outline.description: Sets out the alleged pump-and-dump scheme, the charges, the district court’s dismissal, and the path of the appeal.
subtopics: Who the defendants are and their social-media based trading personas
Alleged scheme mechanics: buy, misrepresent to followers to induce buying, artificially inflate price, sell secretly for profit
Key allegations of deception: false statements about trading positions and price potential
Alleged proceeds of the scheme: approximately $114 million
Charges: conspiracy to commit securities fraud (18 U.S.C. § 1349) and securities fraud (18 U.S.C. §§ 1348 & 2); Knight’s guilty plea; others move to dismiss
District court ruling: dismissal for failure to allege deprivation of a traditional property interest (viewing the theory as about economic information)
Government’s timely appeal to the Fifth Circuit

outline.chapter_title: Standards and Substantive Law Governing the Indictment
outline.description: Explains the de novo standard for testing indictment sufficiency and the elements of securities fraud under § 1348 as informed by mail/wire fraud jurisprudence.
subtopics: Indictment sufficiency on a motion to dismiss: allegations taken as true; must allege each material element; fair notice and double jeopardy functions (Rafoi, Fontenot, Gaytan, Guzman-Ocampo)
Text and scope of 18 U.S.C. § 1348: schemes to defraud and schemes to obtain money or property in connection with securities transactions
Borrowing from mail and wire fraud law to construe § 1348 (Greenlaw)
Core elements: scheme to defraud and intent to defraud (Evans/Greenlaw framework)
Material misrepresentation and the requirement that obtaining money or property be an object of the scheme
Conspiracy under § 1349 rises or falls with the sufficiency of the underlying § 1348 fraud theory

outline.chapter_title: Scheme to Defraud: Property-Based Fraud vs. the Right-to-Control Theory
outline.description: Analyzes why the indictment alleges a traditional property-based fraudulent-inducement scheme rather than the right-to-control theory rejected in Ciminelli.
subtopics: Ciminelli’s holding: the right-to-control theory is not a valid basis for federal fraud; valuable economic information alone is not traditional property
Government’s theory here: fraudulent-inducement—using material misstatements to induce followers to part with money to buy securities
Why the indictment targets money or property: allegations that posts were designed to spur purchases, causing victims to transfer cash for securities
Supreme Court’s clarification that fraudulent-inducement protects money and property and is distinct from right-to-control (Kousisis)
Application to the pleadings: specific misrepresentations (trading positions, price predictions) and secret dumping sufficiently allege a scheme to obtain victims’ money
Satisfaction of the § 1348 “in connection with” requirement: misrepresentations linked to induced securities purchases

outline.chapter_title: Intent to Defraud: Profit Motive, Harm, and the Impact of Kousisis
outline.description: Explores the mental-state requirement and why the defendants’ profit-seeking intent suffices even absent alleged net economic loss to victims.
subtopics: Intent to defraud defined: intent to deceive and intent to cause harm from the deceit (Evans/Greenlaw)
Kousisis’s rule: fraud is complete when the defendant schemes to obtain the victim’s money or property through material deception; no need to seek net pecuniary loss
Application: the indictment alleges defendants posted false information to induce purchases—showing they had money in mind and aimed to obtain victims’ funds
Why receipt of market-value securities by followers does not defeat intent or injury under fraudulent-inducement (Kousisis)
Fifth Circuit support that loss need not mirror defendant’s gain (Baker) and alignment with other circuits post-Kousisis (Seventh Circuit Smith)
Use of the indictment’s language (e.g., Indictment ¶ 13) to illustrate specific allegations of deceitful inducement to purchase

outline.description: States the court’s decision and explains its practical and doctrinal implications for § 1348 prosecutions involving social-media-driven trading schemes.
subtopics: Holding: the indictment adequately alleges both a scheme to defraud and intent to defraud
Disposition: reversal of the district court’s dismissal and remand for further proceedings
What survives a motion to dismiss: sufficiency of pleaded elements; evidentiary proof reserved for trial
Key takeaway: fraudulent-inducement is a valid theory under § 1348; Ciminelli bars right-to-control but not property-focused inducement schemes
Practical implications for social-media promoters and traders: misrepresenting trading positions/intentions to spur purchases can satisfy § 1348

Guidance for drafting and challenging indictments post-Ciminelli and Kousisis: clearly allege material deception, a money-or-property objective, and intent to obtain funds in connection with securities transactions
